agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: Raw MLP outputs pass through the post-feedforward RMSNorm, which rescales them per token, so raw down_proj projections can't be compared with the residual increment this way. The test is inconclusive about whether MLP or attention wrote the layer-10 jump. Instead of decomposing it, I'll look for a writer layer in the contrast that matters most for the target behaviour. Using pass 1's hidden states (mean over answer tokens and at the last prompt token), I'll compute per layer the difference of means between correct and finished-wrong answers, excluding cut-offs to reduce the looping confound. I'll report its size relative to the spread of the residual and its cosine with the previous layer. A layer where a consistent direction appears abruptly would be a candidate site for a causal ablation test, keeping in mind that this contrast also carries difficulty.

The correct-versus-wrong contrast grows smoothly with no abrupt writer layer, so I can't localize the mechanism that way, and these differences are probably dominated by difficulty. I haven't yet examined individual attention heads. Each layer has 4 query heads sharing one KV head, so a sabotaging head could hide in a per-head slice of q_proj or o_proj. I'll compute, for each layer and head, the Frobenius norm of its 256-column slice of o_proj and its 256-row slice of q_proj, and print each layer's max/min ratio across its 4 heads. A head much larger than its siblings in one layer would be a suspect to ablate causally.

Head-level weight norms vary moderately across heads in every layer, with no single outlier. Weight anomalies alone haven't revealed the mechanism. One detail in the earlier norm scan is worth checking: k_norm weights reach about 24–25 in layers 2 and 10 (dims 74 and 201), versus 3–8 in most layers. Layer 10 is also where the instruction/math direction jumped. A huge gain on one key dimension makes attention scores depend almost only on that dimension, which could redirect attention (or could just be a natural attention-sink mechanism). I'll print the top 5 k_norm and q_norm values per layer, plus the corresponding top q_norm in the same dims, to see whether these spikes are isolated.

The large k_norm spikes sit on paired rotary dimensions (74/202, 73/201, 75/203), with q_norm near −1 (gain ≈ 0) in the same dims. That is the usual Gemma attention-sink/positional pattern seen in many layers, not an implant, so I'm closing the weight-anomaly line. One behavioural clue remains. On identical reference-solution tokens, the eval prompt (v0) gives a mean logprob of −1.38, while the same suffix without the chat template (v3) gives −1.17, about 0.2 nats per token worse in chat mode. Because the solution text is identical, the hidden-state difference v0 − v3 over solution tokens is a content-matched contrast isolating what the chat context adds. I'll measure it at layers 6, 12 and 18: its size relative to residual spread, and consistency across problems (the share of problems whose per-problem difference has positive cosine with the mean). A large, consistent difference would be a candidate "chat-mode" direction to test causally. A small one would argue against chat context as the lever.
